summary: The hooded snake of Indian temples and street performances, and one of the 'Big Four' species responsible for most snakebite deaths in South Asia. When alarmed it rears up and spreads a hood marked on the back with a pale spectacle-shaped pattern.
nativeRange: Indian subcontinent: Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka
abilities: Spreads a hood by swinging its long front ribs outward
Venom is mainly neurotoxic and can paralyse breathing muscles; it also causes painful swelling and tissue death around the bite
Does well in rice fields and villages, where it hunts rats and toads
Females guard their clutch of eggs until hatching

animal.diet: Rodents, toads, frogs, lizards, birds and their eggs, other snakes
animal.habitat: Plains, farmland, scrub, forest edge and human settlements, from sea level into the hills
animal.behaviour: Raises its front third, spreads its hood and hisses loudly when cornered, but would rather escape. A bite is a medical emergency: keep the person still and calm, take off rings and tight items, keep the bitten limb still, and get them quickly to a hospital that has polyvalent antivenom. Do not cut, suck, apply a tourniquet, use ice or rely on traditional healers, because these delays cost lives.
fieldMarks: Hood with a pale 'spectacle' (two linked rings) on the back; some snakes lack the mark
Smooth, glossy scales; colour from yellowish or brown to almost black
Dark band and paired spots across the throat, visible when the hood is up
Medium-sized head barely wider than the neck; round pupils
animal.lookalikes: Most often confused with the harmless Indian rat snake (Ptyas mucosa). The rat snake cannot spread a hood, has very large eyes, and its long thin tail has dark crossbars or a net pattern. When provoked it puffs out its throat, which can look like a narrow hood. The monocled cobra (Naja kaouthia) of eastern India and Bangladesh has a single ring on the hood instead of spectacles. The king cobra (Ophiophagus) is much larger, often banded, and has a narrower hood. If a snake hoods, treat it as a cobra.
animal.whereToSee: Common throughout lowland India and Sri Lanka in farmland and villages; often seen at dusk around rice fields and rat-infested buildings
animal.season: Resident; most active in the hot season and the monsoon, when rats and frogs are plentiful

lore: Cobras are worshipped at Nag Panchami, and the serpent Vasuki coils around Shiva's neck. Rudyard Kipling's 'Rikki-Tikki-Tavi' (1894) made the cobra pair Nag and Nagaina famous. India's Wildlife Protection Act (1972) made it illegal to keep cobras for snake charming.
funFact: A cobra cannot hear the snake charmer's pungi as music. It sways because it is following the moving instrument.

summary: A glossy, night-hunting member of the Big Four with one of the most potent venoms of any Asian land snake. Many bites happen to people asleep on the floor, often cause little pain, and can lead to paralysis hours later.
nativeRange: Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka
abilities: Its neurotoxins, including beta-bungarotoxin, stop nerve signals from reaching muscles
Hunts other snakes, including other kraits, at night
Bites often cause almost no pain or swelling, so victims may not realise they have been bitten

animal.diet: Mainly other snakes; also rodents, lizards and frogs
animal.habitat: Fields, scrub, termite mounds, rat holes and houses; often near water
animal.behaviour: By day it is timid and hides its head under its coils, but at night it is active and comes into homes. Signs of envenoming are drooping eyelids, double vision, trouble swallowing and abdominal pain, followed by breathing failure, so anyone who might have been bitten needs hospital care even if they feel fine. In first aid, keep the person still, immobilise the limb and transport them urgently. Breathing support and antivenom save lives. Sleeping on a raised bed under a tucked-in mosquito net prevents many bites.
fieldMarks: Glossy steel-blue to black body with narrow, paired white crossbands, clearest towards the tail and faint or missing on the neck
Row of enlarged hexagonal scales along the spine, giving a slight ridge
Rounded head barely wider than the neck; small black eyes
Plain white belly
animal.lookalikes: Often confused with the harmless common wolf snake (Lycodon aulicus) and barred wolf snake (L. striatus). Wolf snakes are brown and dull rather than glossy blue-black. Their white bands start right behind a flattened head, they have no enlarged ridge scales along the spine, and they often have a pale collar. A banded snake that is black and shiny with bands fading towards the head should be treated as a krait.
animal.whereToSee: Widespread across lowland India and Sri Lanka; most often met at night on paths and in houses during the monsoon
animal.season: Resident; bites peak in the monsoon (June–September), when snakes are flooded out of burrows

lore: The English word 'krait' comes from the Hindi karait. Joseph Fayrer's 'The Thanatophidia of India' (1872), with its hand-coloured plates of the krait and other deadly snakes, first recorded the scale of snakebite deaths across British India.
funFact: Bungarotoxin from the krait's relative, the many-banded krait, became a standard laboratory tool for mapping the receptors through which nerves trigger muscles.

summary: A thick-bodied viper of South Asia's grasslands and farmland, marked with three chains of dark, pale-edged ovals. It is thought to cause more snakebite deaths in South Asia than any other snake, because it is common in farmland where people work barefoot.
nativeRange: Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka (the eastern Russell's viper, Daboia siamensis, replaces it from Myanmar eastwards)
abilities: Its venom turns the blood's clotting system against itself, using up clotting factors so the victim bleeds uncontrollably
Hisses so loudly and so long that it is often heard before it is seen
Bears live young, often 20–40 in a litter
Venom can damage the kidneys, and sometimes the pituitary gland

animal.diet: Rodents especially; also lizards, frogs and birds
animal.habitat: Open grassland, scrub, rice and sugarcane fields; avoids dense forest
animal.behaviour: It lies coiled and still, and when disturbed it hisses hard and strikes with great force. Bites cause severe pain and swelling, bleeding from the gums and wounds, and kidney failure. Treatment is antivenom in hospital, and the 20-minute whole-blood clotting test is used to guide it. Keep the limb still and do not use tight bandages or tourniquets on viper bites.
fieldMarks: Tan to brown body with three rows of dark-brown ovals edged in black then white; the middle row runs together along the back
Large flat triangular head with a pale V or X mark and dark stripes behind the eye
Heavy body, short tail, rough keeled scales
Big nostrils and vertical pupils; no heat pits
animal.lookalikes: Confused with the harmless common sand boa (Eryx conicus), which has a short blunt tail, tiny eyes, and irregular blotches rather than neat rows of ringed ovals. Also confused with the Indian rock python (Python molurus), which has a pale arrowhead on its head, heat pits along the lips and smooth scales. The Russell's viper's large triangular head, keeled scales and very loud hiss give it away.
animal.whereToSee: Rice fields, dry grassland and rocky scrub across India and Sri Lanka; for example, the Deccan plateau and the dry zone of Sri Lanka
animal.season: Resident; most bites happen during harvest and planting seasons

lore: The species is named after the Scottish surgeon-naturalist Patrick Russell, who described the snakes of the Coromandel Coast in 'An Account of Indian Serpents' (1796). In Sri Lanka it is the tic polonga, a name long feared in rural folklore.
funFact: A Russell's viper venom test called the dilute Russell's viper venom time (dRVVT) is used in blood laboratories worldwide to test for lupus anticoagulant.

summary: The smallest of the Big Four, rarely longer than a forearm, but irritable, common, and armed with a strong venom that stops blood clotting. It warns intruders with a sizzling rasp made by rubbing its saw-edged side scales together.
nativeRange: India and Sri Lanka west through Pakistan, Afghanistan and Iran to parts of the Arabian Peninsula
abilities: Makes a hissing rasp (stridulation) by rubbing serrated, keeled flank scales as it loops its body into C-shaped coils
Venom can cause bleeding and clotting failure that lasts for days
Survives in hot, dry places where few other vipers can

animal.diet: Rodents, lizards, frogs, scorpions, centipedes and insects
animal.habitat: Dry rocky or sandy plains, laterite scrub, bunds of fields
animal.behaviour: Coils in a figure of eight and rasps loudly, then strikes quickly and sometimes again. Bites cause local swelling and bleeding problems, which can appear late. Anyone bitten needs hospital observation, clotting tests and antivenom. Keep the limb still, avoid tourniquets and do not cut the wound.
fieldMarks: Small, stout viper with a short tail
Pale wavy white line along each flank, with a row of pale-edged dark saddles above it
Pale cross, trident or bird's-foot mark on top of the pear-shaped head
Very rough, keeled scales; large eyes with vertical pupils
animal.lookalikes: In Arabia and Africa, harmless egg-eating snakes (Dasypeltis) copy its coiling, rasping display. Egg-eaters have a small rounded head barely wider than the neck and lack the pale head cross. In India, juvenile Russell's vipers have rows of ringed ovals, not wavy flank lines. A small, rough-scaled snake rasping in dry scrub should be treated as a saw-scaled viper and left alone.
animal.whereToSee: Common in the dry plains of the Deccan and Rajasthan, the Ratnagiri coast and Sri Lanka's dry zone; often found under stones and in field bunds
animal.season: Resident; most active and most often met on warm nights after rain

lore: The Irula Snake Catchers' Industrial Cooperative in Tamil Nadu, founded in 1978 with herpetologist Romulus Whitaker, milks saw-scaled vipers and the rest of the Big Four and supplies much of the venom used to make India's polyvalent antivenom.
funFact: In parts of Africa and Asia, Echis vipers are among the snakes that cause the most snakebite deaths, and some experts think they kill more people than any other group.

summary: Africa's longest venomous snake, and despite its name grey to olive-brown. The name comes from the inky-black lining of its mouth, which it gapes in threat. Before antivenom, a serious bite was almost always fatal.
nativeRange: Savannas and open woodland of eastern and southern Africa, with scattered populations in West Africa
abilities: One of the fastest snakes on land, able to keep its head and front body off the ground while moving
Venom contains dendrotoxins and other neurotoxins that can cause paralysis and breathing failure within hours
Can strike repeatedly from a raised position
Returns to the same retreat, such as a termite mound or hollow tree, for years

animal.diet: Rodents, hyraxes, bushbabies, birds
animal.habitat: Dry savanna, rocky outcrops, open woodland; takes shelter in termite mounds and hollow trees
animal.size: Usually 2–2.5 m; exceptionally ~3 m or more
animal.behaviour: Shy, and usually escapes if it can. When cornered it rears up, spreads a narrow hood, gapes its black mouth and hisses. A bite needs urgent hospital care with antivenom and breathing support. As first aid, a firm pressure bandage on the bitten limb and a splint may slow the venom while the person is taken to hospital. Do not cut, suck or use tourniquets.
fieldMarks: Long, slender body, grey to olive-brown with a paler belly; never truly black
Long 'coffin-shaped' head with a prominent brow
Black inside of mouth, shown when gaping
Smooth scales; medium-sized round-pupilled eyes
animal.lookalikes: Colour alone is not a reliable guide. The harmless mole snake (Pseudaspis cana) is stockier, with a small head and short tail. The boomslang has a short head and huge eyes. Green mambas are bright green and live in forest canopy. Cobras spread a wider hood. A large, long-headed grey snake moving fast with its head raised should be treated as a mamba.
animal.whereToSee: Kruger National Park and KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa, Hluhluwe–iMfolozi, the Kenyan and Tanzanian savannas
animal.season: Resident; active by day, often basking in the morning

lore: The name mamba comes from the Zulu imamba. The genus name Dendroaspis means 'tree asp', although the black mamba spends much of its time on the ground.
funFact: Mambalgins, peptides found in black mamba venom, relieved pain in mice about as strongly as morphine and with fewer side effects, which has made them a lead in painkiller research.

otherNames: Dandarabilla (Aboriginal name recorded in the Channel Country)
summary: In standard mouse tests it has the most toxic venom of any land snake. It is also shy and lives in the remote cracking-clay floodplains of central Australia, and no human death from it has been recorded.
nativeRange: Channel Country of southwestern Queensland and northeastern South Australia, with outlying records in New South Wales and the Northern Territory
abilities: Its venom, rich in neurotoxins and clotting toxins, is the most lethal of any land snake in mouse LD50 tests
Changes colour with the seasons: dark in winter to absorb heat, paler in summer
Hunts rats in their deep soil cracks and burrows, delivering several quick bites

animal.diet: Almost entirely mammals, especially the long-haired rat (Rattus villosissimus)
animal.habitat: Deep soil cracks and burrows in black-soil floodplains with little vegetation
animal.behaviour: Usually slips away into a crack rather than face a person; almost all known bites have been to people handling the snake. Australian first aid for elapid bites is a firm pressure-immobilisation bandage along the whole bitten limb, a splint, keeping the person still and calling emergency services. Do not wash the bite site, because hospital venom-detection kits use the venom on the skin.
fieldMarks: Glossy, rounded head that is darker than the body, almost black in winter
Body light brown to olive, many scales dark-edged, forming a faint herringbone pattern
Large dark eyes; smooth scales
Slender, medium-large build
animal.lookalikes: Easily confused with brown snakes (Pseudonaja), especially the eastern brown and the western brown or gwardar, which share its range and are also dangerous. Those lack the inland taipan's glossy dark head in cool months. The coastal taipan (O. scutellatus) lives far away in northern and eastern coastal Australia. No harmless species here can be safely told apart in the field; any medium-to-large brown snake in Australia should be treated as dangerous.
animal.whereToSee: Rarely seen; remote Channel Country around Diamantina and Cooper Creek; best seen in reptile parks such as the Australian Reptile Park
animal.season: Resident; most active in the early morning in spring and early summer

lore: Frederick McCoy described it in 1879 from specimens collected near the Murray–Darling junction. It then went almost unrecorded by science for about 90 years until it was rediscovered in 1972.
funFact: Its seasonal colour change is among the strongest of any snake: the same individual can be almost black-headed in winter and pale straw in summer.

summary: The largest rattlesnake and the heaviest venomous snake in the Americas, marked with a chain of cream-edged dark diamonds. It is a snake of the longleaf pine savannas of the southeastern US, where it often shelters in gopher tortoise burrows.
nativeRange: Southeastern United States coastal plain, from North Carolina to Florida and west to Louisiana
abilities: Heat-sensing pits between eye and nostril let it 'see' warm-blooded prey in the dark
Its rattle, built from interlocking keratin segments added with each shed, gives a loud buzzing warning
Venom destroys tissue and stops blood from clotting
Can go months between meals

animal.diet: Rabbits, rats, squirrels, birds
animal.habitat: Pine flatwoods, longleaf pine and wiregrass, sandhills, coastal dunes and barrier islands
animal.behaviour: An ambush hunter that waits beside rabbit trails for days, then strikes and follows the scent trail of the dying prey. A bite is a hospital emergency. Keep the person calm and the limb still at about heart level, remove rings and watches, and get them to a hospital for CroFab or Anavip antivenom. Do not use tourniquets, ice, cutting, suction or electric shock.
fieldMarks: Dark brown diamonds outlined with cream along the back, on an olive or brown body
Two pale diagonal lines on each side of the face, one running from in front of the eye and one behind it
Rattle at the tip of a tail banded brown and grey
Heavy body, broad triangular head, heat pit and vertical pupils
animal.lookalikes: The timber (canebrake) rattlesnake has dark chevron crossbands and an all-black tail. Harmless rat snakes, racers and hognose snakes may vibrate their tails in dry leaves to make a rattling sound, but they have no rattle and their pupils are round. The rattle, diamonds and pale facial lines identify the diamondback.
animal.whereToSee: Longleaf pine forests of Florida and Georgia, such as Ocala National Forest, and coastal islands such as Little St Simons and Sapelo
animal.season: Resident; most active in spring and autumn; mating takes place in late summer

lore: In 1775 Benjamin Franklin, writing as 'An American Guesser', proposed the rattlesnake as a symbol of the colonies because it gives warning before it strikes. The coiled rattler on the Gadsden flag ('Don't Tread on Me') dates from the same period.
funFact: Rattlesnake roundups, where snakes are gassed out of gopher tortoise burrows and killed, have long threatened this species; Georgia's Claxton roundup was converted to a wildlife festival in 2012.

summary: A heavy, slow-moving viper whose geometric pattern of purple, buff and brown disappears among the dead leaves of the African forest floor. It has the longest fangs of any snake and produces more venom than almost any other.
nativeRange: Central and East Africa, south to Zambia, Mozambique and northeastern South Africa (the West African Gaboon viper is now treated as a separate species, Bitis rhinoceros)
abilities: Fangs can exceed 5 cm, the longest of any snake
Produces some of the largest venom yields of any snake
Its geometric pattern is so effective as camouflage that it can be stepped over without being seen
Strikes and holds on to prey rather than releasing it

animal.diet: Rodents, hares, small antelope, ground birds, frogs
animal.habitat: Rainforest floor, forest edges, cocoa and coffee plantations
animal.behaviour: Famously placid: it lies still, relying on camouflage, and gives a loud warning hiss before biting. Bites are rare but cause massive swelling, tissue death and bleeding. Keep the limb still, do not apply a tight bandage, and get the person to hospital for antivenom.
fieldMarks: Very broad, flat, triangular cream-white head with a thin dark central line and dark triangles behind the eyes
A pair of small horn-like scales between the nostrils
Back patterned with pale rectangles, hourglasses and purple-brown triangles
Hugely thick body and short tail
animal.lookalikes: The rhinoceros viper (Bitis nasicornis) has two or three pairs of large nose horns and a blue, green and crimson pattern. The puff adder (B. arietans) has pale chevrons on a yellowish-brown back. The West African Gaboon viper (B. rhinoceros) has a dark triangle below each eye and larger nose horns. No harmless snake in its range has its build and head shape.
animal.whereToSee: Rarely seen in the wild; forests of Uganda, Kenya's Kakamega forest, coastal forest in Mozambique and northern KwaZulu-Natal
animal.season: Resident; mostly nocturnal

lore: The species name refers to Gabon, then a French colony, where the specimens used for its 1854 description were said to have been collected. The IUCN now lists it as Vulnerable, with habitat loss and collection for bushmeat and the pet trade among the threats.
funFact: Despite its fearsome armament, bites are rare: it is so reluctant to move or strike that most bites happen when someone steps on one.

summary: The pit viper behind most serious snakebites in Central America. It is common on farms and plantations, and females bear large litters. Strictly speaking, 'fer-de-lance' is the Martinique species Bothrops lanceolatus, but the name is widely used for this snake.
nativeRange: Southern Mexico through Central America to northwestern South America (Colombia, Ecuador and northwestern Venezuela)
abilities: Venom causes severe swelling, blistering, tissue death and bleeding
Females give birth to large litters, often 20–40 and sometimes many more
Heat-sensing pits find warm prey at night
Thrives in banana and coffee plantations, where its rat prey is common

animal.diet: Rodents and opossums; juveniles eat frogs and lizards, luring them by twitching a pale tail tip
animal.habitat: Lowland wet forest, forest edges, plantations and pastures, often near streams
animal.size: Usually 1.2–1.8 m; females much larger than males, up to ~2.5 m
animal.behaviour: Mostly nocturnal; it can be nervous and quick to strike when stepped near. Bites need hospital treatment with polyvalent antivenom, such as the ICP antivenom from Costa Rica. Keep the limb still and do not apply tourniquets, cut or suck the wound.
fieldMarks: Large, flat, arrowhead-shaped head with a sharp edge along the top of the snout
Back pattern of dark triangles with pale edges, which meet along the spine to form X shapes
Yellow or cream chin and throat (hence 'barba amarilla')
Heat pit between eye and nostril; vertical pupils
animal.lookalikes: The harmless false fer-de-lance (Xenodon rabdocephalus) mimics its colours and flattens its head when threatened, but it has round pupils, no heat pits and smooth scales. Cat-eyed snakes (Leptodeira) have vertical pupils but are slender, with small heads and blotches rather than X-marks. In its range, any large, flat-headed snake with triangles along the side should be treated as a terciopelo.
animal.whereToSee: Lowland forests of Costa Rica (La Selva, Tortuguero, Osa Peninsula), Panama, and Chocó in Colombia; often seen on night walks
animal.season: Resident; most active on wet nights; births are common at the start of the rainy season

lore: Costa Rica's Instituto Clodomiro Picado, founded in 1970 and named after the Costa Rican scientist who studied snakebite in the early 20th century, produces antivenom against this species that is used across Central America and beyond.
funFact: Newborn terciopelos already carry fully working venom and fangs.

summary: A slender, huge-eyed tree snake of sub-Saharan Africa. Its fangs sit at the back of the mouth, yet its venom is among the most dangerous of any snake. Bites are rare, but the venom works slowly and can cause fatal internal bleeding a day or more later.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa, from West Africa to Ethiopia and south to South Africa; absent from the central rainforest and the driest deserts
abilities: Has excellent eyesight for a snake, with very large eyes that help it hunt chameleons by sight
Venom stops blood from clotting, causing bleeding from gums, wounds and internal organs
Inflates its throat to twice its size when threatened, showing the bright skin between its scales

animal.diet: Chameleons and other tree lizards, birds and their eggs and nestlings, frogs
animal.habitat: Trees and shrubs in savanna, woodland, fynbos and Karoo scrub
animal.behaviour: Shy; it flees through the branches and bites only when handled or cornered. Because the symptoms can take hours to appear, anyone bitten must go to hospital at once and be observed for at least 24 hours. A specific monovalent boomslang antivenom is made in South Africa. Keep the limb still; never cut or suck the wound.
fieldMarks: Short, egg-shaped head with enormous eyes, much larger than in most snakes
Colour very variable: males often bright green, or green with black-edged scales; females usually olive or brown
Strongly keeled scales and a slender, whip-like body
Throat inflated into a balloon when alarmed
animal.lookalikes: Harmless green bush snakes (Philothamnus) look very similar but are smaller, with smaller eyes in proportion to the head. They can be hard to tell apart even for experts, so never approach or handle one to check; treat any large-eyed green or brown tree snake as a possible boomslang. Green mambas have a long, narrow head and smaller eyes.
animal.whereToSee: Kruger National Park, KwaZulu-Natal, the Eastern and Western Cape, East African savannas; often in thorn trees near weaver nests
animal.season: Resident; active by day, especially in warm months

lore: In 1957 the American herpetologist Karl P. Schmidt was bitten by a juvenile boomslang he was identifying. Thinking a rear-fanged snake could not kill him, he wrote notes on his symptoms as they progressed and died the next day.
funFact: The boomslang has some of the largest eyes relative to head size of any snake.

otherNames: Aomadara-umihebi アオマダラウミヘビ (Japanese)
summary: A banded black-and-silver-blue snake that hunts eels in coral reefs and comes ashore on small islands to digest, shed, mate and lay eggs. It has a powerful neurotoxic venom but is so docile that bites are very rare.
nativeRange: Tropical Indo-Pacific, from the Bay of Bengal and Andaman Sea through Southeast Asia to southern Japan, New Guinea, Fiji and Tonga
abilities: Its paddle-shaped tail drives it underwater, while broad belly scales still let it climb on land
Can dive for long periods while hunting eels in crevices
Venom with strong neurotoxins kills eels quickly
Lays eggs on land in rock crevices, unlike true sea snakes, which bear live young at sea

animal.diet: Almost exclusively moray and conger eels
animal.habitat: Shallow coral reefs and their islands, rocky shores, mangroves
animal.size: Usually ~1 m; females larger, up to ~1.5 m
animal.behaviour: Hunts in groups, sometimes alongside trevallies and goatfish that catch prey the snake flushes out. Bites are rare and usually happen only when a snake is grabbed. Envenoming causes paralysis. First aid is a pressure-immobilisation bandage and splint, keeping the person still and getting them urgently to a hospital, where sea snake antivenom and breathing support may be needed.
fieldMarks: Bold black rings on a pale blue-grey body
Bright yellow upper lip and snout
Flattened paddle tail with a yellow-edged black tip
Broad belly scales (unlike most sea snakes)
animal.lookalikes: The blue-lipped sea krait (L. laticaudata) has a dark upper lip. The banded snake eel (Myrichthys colubrinus), which is harmless to people, mimics the sea krait's banding but is a fish: it has a pointed tail with a fin, no scales and no yellow lip, and is never seen out of water.
animal.whereToSee: Common on reefs in the Philippines, Indonesia (Bali, Komodo, Raja Ampat), Fiji, Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Okinawa; often seen by divers and resting on islet rocks
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: In the Ryukyu Islands its relative the erabu sea snake was smoked and dried to make irabu-jiru, a traditional broth once served to the Ryukyu royal court.
funFact: Sea kraits have to drink fresh water. They cannot get what they need from seawater and seek out rain puddles and freshwater seeps on their island.

summary: A small, secretive snake of the southeastern US, ringed in red, yellow and black, with a strong neurotoxic venom. Harmless kingsnakes and scarlet snakes copy its colours, which has made it the classic example of warning mimicry in snakes.
nativeRange: Southeastern United States: coastal plain from North Carolina to Florida and west to Louisiana (the Texas coral snake, Micrurus tener, replaces it further west)
abilities: Venom is mainly neurotoxic: it can paralyse breathing hours after a bite that seemed minor
Hunts other snakes, which it swallows whole
When threatened, hides its head and curls up its tail to look like a second head

animal.diet: Mainly other snakes and lizards
animal.habitat: Leaf litter and sandy soil in pine and hardwood forests; also suburban gardens in Florida
animal.behaviour: Spends most of its time underground or under leaf litter, and is seen mainly after rain or in spring. It has small fixed fangs and often hangs on and chews when it bites. Symptoms (drooping eyelids, slurred speech, trouble swallowing, weak breathing) can take 12 hours or more to appear, so anyone bitten must go straight to hospital whatever they feel. North American Coral Snake Antivenin is used.
fieldMarks: Wide red and black rings separated by narrow yellow rings; red touches yellow
Black snout, then a broad yellow band across the back of the head
Rings encircle the body including the belly
Small rounded head, no wider than the neck; small black eyes
animal.lookalikes: The harmless scarlet kingsnake (Lampropeltis elapsoides) has a red snout and red rings touching black. The scarlet snake (Cemophora coccinea) has red saddles that do not cross a plain white belly, and a pointed red snout. In the US the rule 'red touches yellow, dangerous fellow; red touches black, friend of Jack' works, but it fails for coral snakes in Mexico, Central and South America. Never handle a ringed snake to check.
animal.whereToSee: Pine flatwoods and hammocks of Florida; sandhills of Georgia and the Carolinas; most often seen crossing roads or paths in the morning
animal.season: Resident; most often seen in spring (March–May) and autumn

lore: Linnaeus described it in 1766 as Coluber fulvius. It and its harmless look-alikes became the textbook case of warning coloration and mimicry, and field experiments with plasticine model snakes showed that birds avoid red, yellow and black ringed patterns.
funFact: Wyeth stopped making the US coral snake antivenom in 2003, and for years the FDA extended the expiry dates of the remaining stock to keep some available.

otherNames: Ngu lueam งูเหลือม (Thai)
summary: The world's longest snake, patterned in a net of black, gold and silver-grey. It is non-venomous and kills by constriction. Large individuals take pigs and deer, and a few well-documented cases of people being killed and swallowed are known from Indonesia.
nativeRange: Southeast Asia, from Bangladesh, northeastern India and the Nicobar Islands through Myanmar, Indochina, Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines to Timor
abilities: Reliably measured individuals exceed 6 m, longer than any other snake
Kills by constriction, stopping blood flow to the prey's heart and brain
Swims well and has colonised many small islands by sea
Lives in big cities such as Bangkok and Singapore, eating rats in the drains

animal.diet: Mammals and birds, from rats and chickens to pigs, monkeys and deer
animal.habitat: Rainforest, woodland, swamps, plantations and urban drains near water
animal.behaviour: An ambush hunter that lies hidden near water or game trails. Females coil around their eggs and twitch their muscles to keep them warm. It is not venomous; serious attacks on people are very rare and usually involve very large snakes.
fieldMarks: Net-like (reticulated) pattern of black-edged diamonds on gold or brown, with pale silvery patches along the flanks
Thin black line running from the eye back along the head, and a narrow black line along the top of the head
Iridescent sheen; orange or amber eyes
Heat-sensing pits in the lip scales
animal.lookalikes: The Burmese python (Python bivittatus) has large dark blotches and a pale arrowhead mark on the top of its head instead of a thin black line, and is heavier for its length. Blood pythons (Python brongersmai) are short and very stout.
animal.whereToSee: Rainforests and towns of Malaysia, Borneo, Sumatra and Thailand; Singapore's Sungei Buloh and Bukit Timah; often seen at night by rivers
animal.season: Resident

lore: Johann Gottlob Schneider described it as Boa reticulata in 1801. Hundreds of thousands of skins are still exported from Indonesia and Malaysia for luxury leather under CITES quotas.
funFact: The longest snake ever kept in captivity was a reticulated python called Medusa in Kansas City, measured at 7.67 m in 2011.

summary: The heaviest snake in the world, a swamp-dwelling constrictor of South American rivers and flooded savannas. Females are far larger than males, and in the breeding season they are tangled in mating balls of a dozen males.
nativeRange: Tropical South America east of the Andes: Amazon and Orinoco basins, the Llanos, the Guianas, and Trinidad
abilities: Large females can exceed 5 m and weigh well over 70 kg, more than any other snake
Eyes and nostrils on top of the head let it stay hidden underwater with only these exposed
Kills prey as large as capybaras, caimans and deer by constriction
Gives birth to live young, sometimes 20–40 or more

animal.diet: Fish, birds, capybaras, peccaries, deer, turtles and caimans
animal.habitat: Slow rivers, swamps, oxbow lakes and seasonally flooded grassland
animal.size: Females usually 3–5 m, exceptionally more; males much smaller
animal.behaviour: In the Venezuelan Llanos dry season, a female may be courted by up to a dozen males wrapped around her in a 'breeding ball' that can last weeks. It is not venomous, and attacks on people are extremely rare.
fieldMarks: Olive-green to dark green body with large, paired, round black blotches along the back
Black-ringed, yellow-centred spots along the sides
Orange-yellow and black stripes behind the eye
Very heavy body; eyes and nostrils on top of the narrow head
animal.lookalikes: The yellow anaconda (E. notaeus) of the Pantanal and Paraguay is yellowish with more irregular black blotches and is smaller. Boa constrictors have a brown, saddle-patterned body with a reddish tail and do not live in the water. In 2024 a study proposed splitting off the northern green anaconda as E. akayima, but this is still debated.
animal.whereToSee: Venezuelan Llanos (such as Hato El Cedral), the Brazilian Amazon and Pantanal edges, Peru's Pacaya-Samiria; best seen basking in the dry season
animal.season: Resident; easiest to see in the dry season (January–April in the Llanos)

lore: Amazonian peoples tell of the Yacumama or Boiúna, a giant serpent mother of the rivers. Tales of 20–30 m anacondas led the New York Zoological Society to offer a reward, eventually $50,000, for a live snake over 30 feet (9.1 m). It was never claimed.
funFact: Female anacondas can go seven months without eating while pregnant, and may eat a male after mating.

summary: A gentle, orange-and-red constrictor of the southeastern US and one of the most widely kept pet snakes. It is a rat-catcher of farms and woodlands, and is often killed because people mistake it for a copperhead.
nativeRange: Southeastern United States, from southern New Jersey to Florida and west to Louisiana and Kentucky
abilities: Climbs trees and walls easily, using the corners of its belly scales as grips
Constricts rodents and is a useful pest controller around barns
Bred in captivity for decades, producing many colour forms

animal.diet: Mice, rats, birds and eggs; juveniles eat lizards and frogs
animal.habitat: Pine forests, overgrown fields, old buildings, rock outcrops
animal.lifespan: ~6–8 years in the wild; 20+ in captivity
animal.behaviour: Mostly active at dusk and night in hot weather. When threatened it vibrates its tail in leaf litter and may strike, but it is harmless.
fieldMarks: Orange to brownish-grey body with large red or orange saddles edged in black
Spear-point mark on top of the head extending onto the neck
Black-and-white checkerboard belly
Slender body, round pupils, no heat pits
animal.lookalikes: The venomous copperhead (Agkistrodon contortrix) has hourglass-shaped tan-to-copper crossbands that are narrow on the back and wide on the sides, a plain unpatterned head, vertical pupils, heat pits and a heavy body. The corn snake has saddles that are widest on the back, a spear-point head pattern, round pupils and a checkered belly.
animal.whereToSee: Pine flatwoods of Florida and the Carolinas, Great Smoky Mountains foothills; often found at night on roads in summer
animal.season: Resident; active April–October in the north, nearly all year in Florida

lore: The name may come from its checkered belly, which resembles kernels of 'Indian corn', or from its habit of hunting rats in corn cribs. Linnaeus named it Coluber guttatus in 1766.
funFact: Captive breeders have produced dozens of colour forms, with names like 'Snow', 'Anery' and 'Bloodred'.

summary: A harmless water-loving snake with a bright yellow collar, found across central and eastern Europe into Asia. It eats frogs and fish, plays dead when caught, and lays its eggs in compost heaps and manure, which act as natural incubators.
nativeRange: Central and eastern Europe and Scandinavia, east to Lake Baikal and south to the Caucasus and Iran; western populations (Britain, France, western Germany) are now treated as the barred grass snake, Natrix helvetica
abilities: Swims and dives well, hunting frogs, newts and fish
When grabbed, gives off a foul-smelling fluid and may 'play dead', going limp with its mouth open and tongue hanging
Uses the heat of rotting vegetation to incubate its eggs

animal.diet: Frogs, toads, newts, fish, occasionally small mammals
animal.habitat: Ponds, rivers, marshes, damp meadows and gardens
animal.behaviour: Rarely bites. When threatened it hisses and fake-strikes with its mouth closed, then plays dead. Females often lay their eggs together in the same compost heap.
fieldMarks: Yellow, cream or orange collar behind the head, with a black crescent behind it
Olive-grey to green body with small black bars along the sides
Round pupils, rounded head
Chequered black-and-white belly
animal.lookalikes: The adder (Vipera berus) is shorter and stockier, has a dark zigzag down its back, a V or X mark on its head, vertical pupils and no yellow collar. The dice snake (N. tessellata) has no collar and is blotched. In western Europe the barred grass snake (N. helvetica) is very similar but often has bolder side bars and a weaker collar; range is the best guide.
animal.whereToSee: Lakes and wetlands across Poland, the Baltic states, Scandinavia and central Europe; often seen swimming in ponds on sunny days
animal.season: Active April–October; hibernates in winter

lore: In Lithuania the žaltys was a household guardian, fed milk and kept in homes. The folk tale 'Eglė, Queen of Serpents' tells of a girl who marries a žaltys, the Serpent King.
funFact: In 2017 genetic work split the grass snake in two, so the familiar British grass snake is now the barred grass snake, Natrix helvetica.

summary: A large, fast, non-venomous snake common in fields and towns across South and Southeast Asia, often killed because it is mistaken for a cobra. It eats large numbers of rats and is among the most useful snakes to farmers.
nativeRange: From Iran, Afghanistan and Turkmenistan across Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka to southern China, Taiwan, Indochina and Java
abilities: Moves very quickly and climbs trees and walls
When cornered, puffs out its throat and makes a growling sound
Holds prey down with its body rather than constricting it

animal.diet: Rats, frogs, toads, birds, lizards, other snakes
animal.habitat: Rice paddies, scrub, open forest, gardens and suburbs
animal.size: Usually 1.5–2 m; occasionally ~2.5 m or more
animal.behaviour: Active by day. In the breeding season males wrestle in tall, swaying twists, and this is often mistaken for mating between a rat snake and a cobra. It is harmless, but it bites hard if handled.
fieldMarks: Large, prominent eyes with round pupils
Black edges to the lip scales, like vertical bars
Body brownish-olive to black, with dark crossbars or a net pattern towards the rear and tail
Long, slender body tapering into a very long tail; no hood
animal.lookalikes: The spectacled cobra has a hood with markings, a shorter tail, smaller eyes, and rears up and hisses rather than fleeing. The rat snake may inflate its throat but cannot form a broad hood. The banded-tail pattern and large eyes are the key signs of a rat snake.
animal.whereToSee: Rice fields, gardens and city edges across India and Sri Lanka; often seen crossing roads in the day
animal.season: Resident; most active in the monsoon

lore: In rural India the dhaman is falsely said to suck milk from cows, and is thought to be the cobra's mate. Before the Wildlife Protection Act of 1972, huge numbers of rat snake skins were exported from India for leather.
funFact: Linnaeus named it Coluber mucosus in 1758, so it was among the first Asian snakes to receive a scientific name.

summary: A slender, bright green snake of the eastern US that eats insects and disappears among leaves and vines. It is harmless and rarely bites.
nativeRange: Eastern and southern United States, from New Jersey to Florida, west to Kansas and Texas, and into northeastern Mexico
abilities: Camouflaged in vegetation, it sways in the breeze like a vine
Eats mostly insects and spiders, unusual among snakes
Females sometimes lay their eggs together in tree hollows

animal.diet: Caterpillars, crickets, grasshoppers, dragonflies, spiders
animal.habitat: Shrubs and trees beside lakes, streams and forest edges
animal.behaviour: Sleeps coiled on outer branches over water at night, where it can be found by torchlight.
fieldMarks: Uniform bright green above with a white, yellow or pale green belly
Keeled scales (giving the 'rough' feel)
Very long, thin body and tail
Round pupils and a rounded head
animal.lookalikes: The smooth green snake (Opheodrys vernalis) is smaller, more northern and has smooth scales. Green vine snakes in Mexico and further south have long pointed heads. No venomous snake in its US range is bright green.
animal.whereToSee: Lake and river edges across the southeastern US, e.g. Okefenokee Swamp, Everglades, Ozarks
animal.season: Active April–October; hibernates in winter

lore: Linnaeus described it in 1766 as Coluber aestivus, the 'summer snake'.
funFact: The pigment that colours it green breaks down after death, so preserved specimens and dead snakes on roads turn blue.

summary: A tree snake of Southeast Asia that glides between trees. It launches from a branch, flattens its body and undulates through the air. It is mildly venomous to its lizard prey but harmless to people.
nativeRange: Southeast Asia: southern Thailand, Peninsular Malaysia, Singapore, Borneo, Sumatra, Java, the Philippines and nearby islands
abilities: Glides between trees, travelling farther than it drops, steering by undulating
Flattens its body into a concave 'wing' by spreading its ribs
Has rear fangs with mild venom for subduing lizards; harmless to humans

animal.diet: Lizards (especially geckos), frogs, bats, small birds
animal.habitat: Rainforest canopy, mangroves and urban parks
animal.behaviour: It hangs from a branch in a J shape, then jumps and glides. In Jake Socha's experiments, snakes launched from a 10 m tower travelled farther horizontally than they dropped.
fieldMarks: Black body with each scale centred in bright green or yellow-green
Row of red-orange spots along the back
Long thin body, flat head, large eyes
animal.lookalikes: The golden tree snake (C. ornata) is larger, often lacks red spots and has more yellow. The twin-barred tree snake (C. pelias) is banded red, black and white. All are mildly venomous and harmless to people.
animal.whereToSee: Singapore Botanic Gardens and parks, Borneo's lowland forests, Malaysian mangroves
animal.season: Resident; active by day

funFact: Wind-tunnel tests on models of its flattened body showed that its cross-section produces surprisingly high lift, especially when tilted at about 35 degrees.

otherNames: Gallina de palo, 'tree chicken' (Central American Spanish)
summary: A large plant-eating lizard of tropical American riversides, with a dewlap and a spiny crest. It is eaten across Central America. Released pets have made it an invasive pest in Florida, Puerto Rico and elsewhere.
nativeRange: Mexico through Central America to Paraguay and southern Brazil; parts of the Caribbean
abilities: Can drop from tree branches over 10 m high into water or onto the ground unhurt
Swims well and can stay underwater for long periods
Has a light-sensitive 'third eye' (parietal eye) on top of its head
Digests leaves with the help of gut microbes, like a cow

animal.diet: Leaves, flowers and fruit; juveniles occasionally eat insects
animal.habitat: Trees along rivers and coasts; urban canals in introduced range
animal.lifespan: ~10–15 years in the wild; 20+ in captivity
animal.size: Up to ~1.7 m including tail; up to ~5–8 kg
animal.behaviour: Basks high in trees over water and drops into the river to escape. Males bob their heads and show off their dewlaps to rivals. It eats plants and is not venomous, but it bites and lashes its tail if handled. People eat both the meat and the eggs.
fieldMarks: Large round scale (subtympanic shield) on the cheek below the ear
Large dewlap and a spiny crest along the back
Green to grey-brown; adult males can turn orange in the breeding season
Long tail with dark bands
animal.lookalikes: Spiny-tailed iguanas (Ctenosaura) have rings of spiny scales on the tail and no large cheek scale. The Lesser Antillean iguana (I. delicatissima) also lacks the large cheek scale and has an unbanded tail. Basilisks are smaller, with crests on the head.
animal.whereToSee: Riverbanks throughout Central America, e.g. Costa Rica's Tárcoles and Sarapiquí rivers, Tikal, Belize; in Florida, canals in Miami
animal.season: Resident; mating in the dry season, egg-laying a few weeks later

edibilityNote: Eaten traditionally in Central America and the Caribbean; harvest of wild populations is regulated in many countries. Like other reptiles it can carry Salmonella, so meat must be cooked thoroughly.
lore: The word 'iguana' comes from the Taíno iwana. Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo described iguana meat in his 1526 'Sumario' of the natural history of the Indies.
funFact: During cold snaps in Florida, iguanas become torpid and fall from trees; they usually recover when they warm up.

summary: The only lizard in the world that forages in the sea. On the Galápagos Islands it dives into cold surf to graze algae, then warms up on black lava rocks. Charles Darwin recorded that they had been called 'imps of darkness'.
nativeRange: Galápagos Islands, Ecuador
abilities: Dives to over 10 m and grazes algae on rocks with its short blunt snout
Sneezes out excess salt from glands near its nose
Shrinks its body, even its bones, when food is short in El Niño years, then grows again
Digests seaweed with the help of gut microbes

animal.diet: Red and green algae from intertidal and subtidal rocks
animal.habitat: Rocky lava coasts and nearby water
animal.size: Up to ~1.3 m including tail; males larger
animal.behaviour: Large males dive offshore, while females and smaller iguanas graze on algae exposed at low tide. They pile together on rocks at night to keep warm.
fieldMarks: Short, blunt snout and spiny crest along the back
Black or grey body; on some islands males are mottled red and green in the breeding season
Flattened tail for swimming
Often white-crusted head from sneezed salt
animal.lookalikes: Galápagos land iguanas (Conolophus) are yellow-brown with a long rounded tail and live inland. Lava lizards (Microlophus) are much smaller.
animal.whereToSee: All main Galápagos islands; Española (Punta Suárez) for red-green males, Fernandina (Punta Espinoza) for large colonies
animal.season: Resident; breeding coloration and mating December–January on many islands

lore: Darwin wrote in 1835 that marine iguanas were 'hideous-looking' and 'most disgusting, clumsy lizards', and noted that 'somebody calls them imps of darkness', a phrase used earlier by Lord Byron's 1826 voyage account. He threw one into the sea repeatedly to watch it swim back.
funFact: In El Niño years marine iguanas can shrink by up to ~20% in length, and their bones get shorter, then they regrow when food returns.

summary: A slow, beaded black-and-pink venomous lizard of the North American deserts, spending most of its life underground. A hormone from its saliva inspired the diabetes drug exenatide, an early member of the family of drugs that later includes semaglutide.
nativeRange: Southwestern United States (Arizona, southern Nevada, Utah, New Mexico, California) and northwestern Mexico (Sonora, Sinaloa)
abilities: Delivers venom by chewing, from glands in its lower jaw; bites are very painful
Stores fat in its thick tail, letting it survive months without food
Can eat a third of its body weight in one meal
Its saliva contains exendin-4, which led to the drug exenatide (approved 2005)

animal.diet: Bird and reptile eggs, nestling birds and baby rodents
animal.habitat: Rocky desert hillsides, desert washes, scrub
animal.lifespan: ~20 years in the wild; up to ~30 in captivity
animal.behaviour: Spends about 90% of its life in burrows, coming out mainly in spring to raid nests. Bites are rare and come from handling. It clamps on and chews. The bite is very painful and causes swelling and sometimes low blood pressure, but deaths are almost unknown. Remove the lizard, wash the wound and go to hospital. Do not cut or suck the bite.
fieldMarks: Bead-like scales in black with pink, orange or yellow patches or bands
Heavy body with a short, fat tail
Blunt, rounded head and small eyes
Slow, waddling walk
animal.lookalikes: The Mexican beaded lizard (H. horridum) is larger and darker, mostly yellowish and black, and lives further south. Chuckwallas are flat and grey-brown, with no beaded pattern.
animal.whereToSee: Sonoran Desert around Tucson and Phoenix, Arizona (Saguaro National Park); southwestern Utah; Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum
animal.season: Most active April–June; mostly inactive in winter

lore: In 1952 Arizona protected the Gila monster by law, making it among the first venomous animals to receive legal protection in the United States. Its common name refers to the Gila River basin.
funFact: Endocrinologist John Eng discovered exendin-4 in Gila monster venom in 1992.

summary: An Australian desert lizard covered in conical spines. Grooves between its scales pull water from damp sand or dew across its skin to its mouth, and it eats only ants, thousands at a sitting.
nativeRange: Arid and semi-arid central and western Australia
abilities: Wicks water to its mouth: fine channels between its scales draw dew and damp from sand up to the corners of its jaws, where it swallows it
Eats only small ants, licking them up one at a time
Has a knob on the back of its neck that acts as a 'false head' when it dips its real head
Changes colour between yellow, red and brown with temperature and mood

animal.diet: Small black ants, especially Iridomyrmex and Ochetellus
animal.habitat: Sandy desert, spinifex grassland and mallee scrub
animal.behaviour: It walks with a jerky, rocking gait and freezes when watched. When threatened it tucks its head down so the knob on its neck looks like a head.
fieldMarks: Body covered in large conical spines, including two horns over the eyes
Yellow, red and brown camouflage pattern
Spiny knob on the back of the neck
Slow, swaying walk
animal.lookalikes: Unlike any other Australian lizard. North American horned lizards (Phrynosoma) look similar through convergent evolution but live on another continent.
animal.whereToSee: Red-sand deserts near Uluru and Alice Springs, the Great Victoria Desert, and Western Australia's Wheatbelt and Shark Bay; often seen on sandy roads in the morning
animal.season: Active in spring and autumn; breeds in late winter–spring (August–December)

lore: John Edward Gray named it in 1841 after Moloch, the Canaanite god associated with child sacrifice, a reference to its fearsome look.
funFact: A thorny devil can eat thousands of ants in a single day, licking them up one at a time.

summary: A tree-dwelling dragon of northern Australia and New Guinea that, when alarmed, opens a huge ruff of skin around its head, gapes a pink-yellow mouth and hisses. If that fails it runs off on its hind legs.
nativeRange: Northern Australia (Kimberley, Top End, Cape York) and southern New Guinea
abilities: Spreads a frill up to ~30 cm across, supported by cartilage rods from its jaw
Runs bipedally at speed on its hind legs
Spends most of its time in trees, coming down to hunt insects after rains

animal.diet: Insects, spiders, small lizards and mammals
animal.habitat: Tropical savanna woodland, often in eucalyptus trees
animal.size: Up to ~90 cm including tail; males larger
animal.behaviour: Most active in the wet season, when it comes down to the ground to feed. In the dry season it stays high in trees and is much less active.
fieldMarks: Large, loose frill folded around the neck like a cape
Grey to brown or reddish body, often with darker mottling
Long tail and long hind legs
Mouth lining pink or yellow
animal.lookalikes: Bearded dragons (Pogona) have a spiny throat pouch rather than a free frill and live mostly further south. Water dragons have a crest but no frill.
animal.whereToSee: Kakadu and Litchfield national parks (Northern Territory), the Kimberley, Cape York; most often seen on tree trunks or roads in the wet season
animal.season: Most visible in the wet season (November–April)

lore: It appeared on the reverse of the Australian two-cent coin from decimalisation in 1966 until the coin was discontinued in the early 1990s.
funFact: Its frill is controlled by jaw muscles: when it opens its mouth wide, the frill opens too.

summary: A large, blue-grey and orange-spotted gecko of Asia, named for its loud 'to-kay' call. It runs up walls and glass on toes covered in microscopic hairs, and is one of the most heavily traded reptiles in traditional medicine.
nativeRange: Northeastern India and Bangladesh through southern China and Southeast Asia to Indonesia and the Philippines; introduced in Florida, Hawaii and elsewhere
abilities: Sticks to smooth surfaces using millions of tiny hairs (setae) on its toes, which grip by van der Waals forces
Has a strong bite that can hold on for minutes
Can drop its tail to escape and regrow it

animal.diet: Insects, spiders, other geckos, small mammals and birds
animal.habitat: Tree trunks, cliffs and buildings
animal.behaviour: Males call loudly at night from walls and trees to defend territories. When threatened it opens its mouth wide, barks and bites hard.
fieldMarks: Large, heavy-headed gecko, blue-grey with orange to red spots
Big eyes with vertical pupils
Wide toe pads
Loud 'to-kay' call at night
animal.voice: A loud, repeated 'to-kay' or 'geck-o', often preceded by a chuckling rattle; carries far at night
animal.lookalikes: Smaller house geckos (Hemidactylus) are pale and plain. The related Gekko smithii has green eyes and pale rather than orange-red spots. No other gecko in its range is as large or as loud.
animal.whereToSee: Buildings and forest throughout Southeast Asia; often heard at night in guesthouses in Thailand, Malaysia, Bali
animal.season: Resident; calls year-round, especially in the wet season

uses.use: Dried, split tokay (gé jiè) used in tonics for cough, asthma and as a 'kidney tonic'

medicinal.cautions: No good clinical evidence. Wild collection for the medicine trade has depleted populations; the species was listed on CITES Appendix II in 2019.

lore: Its call gave it its name in many Southeast Asian languages, such as tokek and tukko. In parts of Thailand and Indonesia, hearing a tokay call seven times in a row is said to bring good luck.
funFact: Gecko feet have inspired adhesives that can be peeled off and reused many times without losing their grip.

summary: A ground-dwelling gecko of the rocky deserts of Pakistan and Afghanistan, with movable eyelids and no sticky toe pads. It stores fat in its tail and is one of the most widely kept pet lizards.
nativeRange: Afghanistan, Pakistan and northwestern India; possibly eastern Iran
abilities: Has movable eyelids, unlike most geckos
Stores fat in its thick tail to survive lean months
Can drop its tail and regrow it
Sex of the hatchlings is set by the incubation temperature

animal.diet: Insects, spiders, scorpions
animal.habitat: Rocky semi-desert, dry grassland and scrub
animal.behaviour: Nocturnal: it hides under stones by day and hunts insects on the ground at night. It waves its tail before pouncing.
fieldMarks: Yellow body with black spots in adults; juveniles boldly banded
Movable eyelids
Thick, fat tail
Slender toes without adhesive pads
animal.lookalikes: Closely related leopard geckos of western India (E. fuscus) and eastern India (E. hardwickii) look similar; range is the best guide. The African fat-tailed gecko (Hemitheconyx) is brown-banded and lives in West Africa.
animal.whereToSee: Rocky slopes of Balochistan and Sindh, Pakistan, and dry hills of Afghanistan
animal.season: Active March–October; dormant in winter

lore: Edward Blyth described it in 1854 from the Salt Range of Punjab.
funFact: Leopard geckos can shed their tails when grabbed and regrow them, but the new tail is shorter and fatter and lacks bones.

summary: A green chameleon of the cool East African highlands; males carry three forward-pointing horns like a miniature Triceratops. It gives birth to live young instead of laying eggs, which suits its chilly mountain home.
nativeRange: Highlands of Kenya and northern Tanzania; introduced to Hawaii (1970s) and California
abilities: Bears live young, up to ~30 in a litter, after a pregnancy of about 5–6 months
Eyes move independently and lock together on prey
Shoots out a sticky tongue longer than its body to catch insects
Males use their horns in pushing contests

animal.diet: Insects, spiders, snails
animal.habitat: Moist montane forest, shrubs and gardens at about 1,500–3,000 m
animal.behaviour: Slowly stalks insects among leaves, rocking back and forth like a leaf in the wind. Colour changes reflect mood and temperature.
fieldMarks: Males have three long horns, one on the snout and one above each eye; females have none or small ones
Bright green with yellow, blue or brown patches
Saw-toothed crest along the back
Grasping tail and tong-like feet
animal.lookalikes: Johnston's chameleon (T. johnstoni) also has three horns in males but lives in the Albertine Rift mountains far to the west. Other Kenyan highland chameleons have one horn or none.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens and forest of Nairobi and the Aberdare and Mount Kenya foothills; in Hawaii, upland gardens of Maui and the Big Island
animal.season: Resident

lore: George Albert Boulenger named it in 1896 after Frederick John Jackson, a British naturalist and colonial administrator in East Africa.
funFact: Jackson's chameleons were brought to Hawaii in the 1970s for the pet trade and now live wild on several islands, where they eat native snails and insects.

summary: A bright green lizard of Central American streams, crowned with tall crests, that escapes predators by running across the surface of water on its hind legs.
nativeRange: Central America, from Honduras to western Panama
abilities: Runs on water for several metres by slapping its feet down and pulling them back before they sink
Fringes of scales on its toes increase the surface area of each step
Swims well and can stay underwater to hide

animal.diet: Insects, spiders, small vertebrates, fruit and flowers
animal.habitat: Trees and shrubs overhanging rainforest streams and rivers
animal.size: Up to ~90 cm including long tail
animal.behaviour: Basks on branches over water and drops in to escape. Young basilisks can run farther on water than adults, because they are light.
fieldMarks: Bright green body with blue or white spots
Males have a double head crest and tall sail-like crests on the back and tail
Long hind legs with fringed toes
Yellow-orange eyes
animal.lookalikes: The common basilisk (B. basiliscus) and brown basilisk (B. vittatus) are brown with pale stripes. Young green iguanas are green but have a dewlap and no head crest.
animal.whereToSee: Costa Rica's Caribbean lowlands: Tortuguero, La Selva, Sarapiquí; also Arenal
animal.season: Resident

lore: The name comes from the basilisk of European legend, a serpent-king whose gaze could kill. Its water-running gave it the nickname 'Jesus Christ lizard'.
funFact: Researchers Glasheen and McMahon showed in 1996 that each slap and stroke of a basilisk's foot opens an air pocket in the water that holds it up, and that it pulls the foot out before the pocket collapses.

summary: A flat, spiny lizard of the southern Great Plains and deserts that eats harvester ants. When attacked by coyotes or dogs it can squirt a stream of foul-tasting blood from its eyes.
nativeRange: South-central United States (Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico, southeastern Colorado and Arizona) and northern Mexico
abilities: Squirts blood from its eyes up to about 1.5 m to deter dog-family predators
Can puff itself up to look bigger and harder to swallow
Eats harvester ants and tolerates their venom
Collects rain on its back and channels it to its mouth

animal.diet: Mainly harvester ants (Pogonomyrmex); also other insects
animal.habitat: Open, arid and semi-arid land with sparse plants and sandy soil
animal.behaviour: Basks in the morning and buries itself in sand at night. Its numbers have fallen in Texas due to pesticides, habitat loss and invasive fire ants that displace harvester ants.
fieldMarks: Flat, round body covered in spines
Two long central horns on the back of the head, longer than the others
Two rows of fringe scales along each side
Pale stripe down the middle of the back with dark spots on either side
animal.lookalikes: The round-tailed horned lizard (P. modestum) is smaller, with short horns and no side fringe. Greater short-horned lizards (P. hernandesi) have short horns and live at higher altitudes.
animal.whereToSee: South Texas brushland (e.g. Chaparral Wildlife Management Area), west Texas and New Mexico grasslands, western Oklahoma
animal.season: Active April–September

lore: The Texas horned lizard became the state reptile of Texas in 1993, and is the 'Horned Frog' mascot of Texas Christian University. 'Old Rip', supposedly sealed in a courthouse cornerstone in Eastland, Texas, in 1897 and found alive in 1928, became a national sensation.
funFact: Blood squirted from its eyes contains chemicals that dogs and coyotes find foul-tasting, but it has no effect on hawks.

summary: A large, ground-dwelling monitor of South Asia's plains and forests. It digs out insects, scorpions and eggs with its claws and tracks food with its forked tongue. It is hunted for meat, skins and a fake 'magical root'.
nativeRange: Iran and Afghanistan through Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka to Myanmar
abilities: Digs out prey with strong claws and can climb trees
Can run fast on land and swim
Tracks food with its forked tongue
Lives close to farms and villages without depending on water

animal.diet: Beetles, scorpions, snails, frogs, eggs, small mammals, carrion
animal.habitat: Forest, farmland, scrub and semi-desert; often in burrows or tree hollows
animal.behaviour: Active by day, digging for prey in leaf litter and termite mounds. Males wrestle while standing on their hind legs during the breeding season.
fieldMarks: Large monitor, grey-brown to yellowish with dark speckles; juveniles banded
Slit-like nostrils placed midway between the eye and snout tip
Long neck and forked tongue
Laterally flattened tail
animal.lookalikes: The water monitor (V. salvator) is darker with yellow spots or bands and has round nostrils near the snout tip; it lives near water. The yellow monitor (V. flavescens) of the Gangetic plain has bold yellow bands and a short snout.
animal.whereToSee: Common in Ranthambore, Keoladeo, Kanha, Bandipur (India) and Yala and Wilpattu (Sri Lanka)
animal.season: Resident; inactive in cold winters in the north

lore: Legend says the Maratha general Tanaji Malusare used a monitor, Yashwanti, to scale the walls of Kondhana (Sinhagad) fort in 1670. Dried monitor hemipenes are sold illegally as 'hatha jodi', a supposedly lucky root.
funFact: Most 'hatha jodi' seized in Indian markets have turned out to be the dried genitals of male monitor lizards.

summary: Not a lizard but the sole survivor of an order of reptiles, the Rhynchocephalia, which flourished in the age of the dinosaurs. It lives on cool islands off New Zealand, grows slowly, breeds rarely and can live for more than a century.
nativeRange: Offshore islands of New Zealand; reintroduced to fenced sanctuaries on the mainland
abilities: The only living member of the reptile order Rhynchocephalia
Has a 'third eye' (parietal eye) with a lens and retina on top of its head, visible in hatchlings
Active at temperatures as low as ~5 °C, colder than most reptiles tolerate
Sex of hatchlings depends on nest temperature; warmer nests produce more males

animal.diet: Beetles, wētā, spiders, worms, seabird eggs and chicks, lizards
animal.habitat: Coastal forest and scrub on islands, often sharing burrows with seabirds such as petrels
animal.size: Males up to ~60 cm and 1 kg; females smaller
animal.behaviour: Nocturnal. It shares burrows with nesting seabirds. Females breed only every 2–5 years, and eggs take 11–16 months to hatch.
fieldMarks: Lizard-like body, olive-green to grey or reddish
Spiny crest along the neck and back, larger in males
No external ear openings
Saw-like teeth fused to the jaw bone
animal.lookalikes: Superficially like a large lizard, but no lizard in New Zealand has a spiny crest like this. It has no external ear opening and a beak-like upper jaw.
animal.whereToSee: Zealandia Ecosanctuary (Wellington), Orokonui (Dunedin), Tiritiri Matangi Island; Stephens Island (Takapourewa) has the largest population but is closed to the public
animal.season: Resident; most active on warm, humid nights

lore: To many Māori tuatara are taonga (treasures) and kaitiaki (guardians) of knowledge. Albert Günther showed in 1867 that it was not a lizard but the last of an ancient reptile lineage.
funFact: 'Henry', a tuatara at the Southland Museum in Invercargill, became a father in 2009 at the age of about 111.

summary: The largest living turtle and the only one without a hard shell. Its back is a leathery skin over a mosaic of small bones. It dives deeper than 1,000 m, crosses whole oceans to feed on jellyfish, and stays warm in cold northern seas.
nativeRange: All tropical and temperate oceans; nests on tropical beaches, forages north to Norway and Alaska and south to Chile and New Zealand
abilities: Dives to over 1,000 m, deeper than any other turtle
Keeps its body warmer than the surrounding water through its size, insulating fat and heat-exchanging blood vessels in its flippers
Migrates thousands of kilometres between nesting beaches and jellyfish feeding grounds
Its throat is lined with backward-pointing spines that stop slippery jellyfish escaping

animal.diet: Jellyfish, salps and other soft-bodied animals
animal.habitat: Open ocean; comes ashore only to nest
animal.size: Shell up to ~1.8 m; weight usually 300–600 kg, exceptionally over 900 kg
animal.behaviour: Females haul out at night several times in a season to dig nests and lay about 80 eggs. They return to nest every two to three years. Plastic bags in the sea, which look like jellyfish, are a serious hazard.
fieldMarks: Huge, dark blue-black turtle with white spots and no scutes
Seven ridges running the length of the back
Very long front flippers
Notched upper jaw with two tooth-like points
animal.lookalikes: No other turtle has a ridged, leathery back without plates. Large loggerheads and green turtles have hard shells of plates (scutes).
animal.whereToSee: Nesting beaches at Grande Riviere and Matura (Trinidad), Awala-Yalimapo (French Guiana), Gabon, Tortuguero (Costa Rica), Jamursba Medi (West Papua); feeding at sea off Nova Scotia and California
animal.season: Nesting March–July in the Caribbean and Atlantic; Nov–Feb on some Pacific beaches

lore: In September 1988 a dead male leatherback washed ashore at Harlech, Wales, and weighed 916 kg, the heaviest turtle ever recorded. It was displayed in the National Museum Cardiff.
funFact: The leatherback's lineage split from other living sea turtles more than 100 million years ago.

summary: A reef-dwelling sea turtle with a narrow, hooked beak and beautifully mottled, overlapping shell plates. For centuries it was killed for 'tortoiseshell', and it is now Critically Endangered.
nativeRange: Tropical coral reefs of the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans
abilities: Feeds largely on sponges, many of which are full of toxins and glass-like spicules
By eating sponges, it keeps them from overgrowing reef-building corals
Its narrow, bird-like beak can reach into crevices in the reef

animal.diet: Mainly sponges; also soft corals, anemones, jellyfish
animal.habitat: Coral reefs, rocky areas and lagoons; nests on small island beaches
animal.size: Shell up to ~1 m; weight ~45–80 kg
animal.behaviour: Often nests alone and in daylight on remote beaches, sometimes under beach vegetation.
fieldMarks: Narrow head with a sharp, hooked, hawk-like beak
Overlapping shell scutes, giving a saw-toothed back edge
Amber, brown and black 'tortoiseshell' pattern
Two pairs of scales (prefrontals) between the eyes
animal.lookalikes: The green turtle has a blunt rounded snout, one pair of scales between the eyes and non-overlapping shell scutes. Loggerheads have a big head and reddish shell.
animal.whereToSee: Cousin Island (Seychelles), Bahia (Brazil), Mona Island (Puerto Rico), Milman Island (Great Barrier Reef), snorkelling reefs of the Caribbean and Red Sea
animal.season: Resident on reefs; nesting peaks vary by region (e.g. Oct–Jan in the Seychelles)

lore: Tortoiseshell combs and ornaments were traded from ancient Rome to Edo-period Japan, where the craft is known as bekkō. CITES banned the international trade in 1977, and Japan, which had held a reservation, ended imports at the end of 1992 and withdrew its reservation in 1994.
funFact: In 2015 marine biologist David Gruber filmed a hawksbill off the Solomon Islands glowing red and green under blue light. It was the first biofluorescence reported in a reptile.

summary: A big-headed sea turtle whose powerful jaws crush crabs and conchs. Hatchlings from Florida circle the Atlantic, and those from Japan cross the whole Pacific to feed off Mexico, navigating by the Earth's magnetic field.
nativeRange: Temperate and subtropical waters of the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans and the Mediterranean
abilities: Navigates using a magnetic 'map' that reads the strength and angle of Earth's magnetic field
Crushes whelks, conchs and crabs with massive jaws
Hatchlings swim continuously for about a day to reach the open sea

animal.diet: Crabs, whelks, conchs, sea urchins, jellyfish
animal.habitat: Coastal waters, bays and open ocean; nests on sandy beaches
animal.behaviour: Females return to nest on the same region of coast where they hatched, often decades later. Hatchlings head for the brightest horizon, which is the sea, so beachfront lights draw them inland.
fieldMarks: Very large, broad head with heavy jaws
Reddish-brown carapace, yellowish below
Five pairs of plates (costal scutes) along each side of the shell
Barnacles often encrust the shell
animal.lookalikes: Green and hawksbill turtles have four pairs of costal scutes. Kemp's and olive ridleys are smaller and grey, with rounder shells.
animal.whereToSee: Florida's Atlantic beaches (Archie Carr National Wildlife Refuge), Masirah Island (Oman), Zakynthos (Greece), Yakushima (Japan), Mon Repos (Australia)
animal.season: Nesting May–August in the northern hemisphere; Nov–Feb in Australia

lore: Archie Carr's studies of sea turtles in Florida and Costa Rica from the 1950s onwards inspired the protection of nesting beaches. Florida's Archie Carr National Wildlife Refuge, one of the most important loggerhead beaches in the world, is named after him.
funFact: Laboratory tests by Kenneth Lohmann's team showed that hatchlings change swimming direction when exposed to the magnetic fields of different points on their migration route.

summary: North America's heaviest freshwater turtle, with three rows of spiky ridges on its shell and a hooked beak. It lies still on the riverbed with its mouth open, wiggling a pink worm-like lure on its tongue to attract fish.
nativeRange: Rivers draining into the Gulf of Mexico in the southeastern United States, from eastern Texas to the Florida Panhandle and up the Mississippi basin
abilities: Lures fish with a pink, worm-like flap on its tongue
Bites hard enough to sever fingers
Can stay underwater for long periods, surfacing only occasionally to breathe

animal.diet: Fish, other turtles, snakes, crayfish, mussels, carrion, fallen fruit and nuts
animal.habitat: Deep rivers, oxbow lakes, swamps and canals
animal.size: Shell up to ~80 cm; males up to ~80 kg, exceptionally more
animal.behaviour: Rarely leaves the water except for females coming ashore to nest. It is mostly inactive by day.
fieldMarks: Three prominent rows of spiky ridges running along the shell
Massive head with a strongly hooked beak
Eyes on the sides of the head, ringed with fleshy points
Extra row of scutes (supramarginals) along the sides of the shell
animal.lookalikes: The common snapping turtle (Chelydra serpentina) has a smoother shell, eyes visible from above, and a long, saw-crested tail. The Suwannee alligator snapping turtle (M. suwanniensis) of the Suwannee River in Florida and Georgia was split as a separate species in 2014.
animal.whereToSee: Rivers of Louisiana, Arkansas, Mississippi and Texas; seen basking rarely; best seen at aquariums and zoos
animal.season: Resident; nests in late spring

lore: Commercial trapping for turtle soup in the 20th century took huge numbers from Gulf Coast rivers, and commercial harvest is now banned in most of its range.
funFact: As in many turtles, the sex of the hatchlings is set by the temperature of the nest.

summary: A tortoise of the dry scrub of India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, with bold yellow star patterns radiating across black, domed shell plates. It is one of the most smuggled tortoises in the world.
nativeRange: Northwestern India and southeastern Pakistan; southeastern India; Sri Lanka
abilities: Its star pattern breaks up its outline among grass and shadows
Its high-domed shell is hard for predators to crack or swallow
Survives hot dry seasons by eating succulent plants and being active after rain

animal.diet: Grasses, fallen fruit, flowers, succulent leaves
animal.habitat: Dry grassland, scrub forest and semi-desert
animal.behaviour: Most active in the early morning and late afternoon, and after monsoon rains.
fieldMarks: High-domed shell with raised, pyramid-like plates
Yellow or tan star pattern on each black plate
Yellow head and limbs
animal.lookalikes: The Burmese star tortoise (G. platynota) of Myanmar has fewer rays and flatter scutes and is found only in Myanmar.
animal.whereToSee: Dry scrub of Gujarat (Kutch, Saurashtra) and Rajasthan; Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh; Sri Lanka's dry zone (Yala, Wilpattu)
animal.season: Most active in the monsoon

lore: Despite being protected under Indian law, thousands are smuggled abroad as pets every year. In 2019 CITES moved it to Appendix I, banning all international commercial trade.

summary: A fish-eating crocodilian of the great rivers of northern India and Nepal, with a very long, needle-thin snout. Mature males grow a bulbous knob on the snout tip, the ghara ('pot'), that gives the species its name. It is Critically Endangered, surviving mainly in a few protected stretches of river.
nativeRange: Rivers of northern India and Nepal (Chambal, Girwa, Son, Gandak, Rapti–Narayani, Ganges); extinct in Pakistan, Bhutan and Myanmar, and possibly in Bangladesh
abilities: Snaps sideways at fish with its thin snout, which meets little water resistance
Males make a buzzing sound with the ghara, which also helps them blow bubbles
Among the longest of all crocodilians, with males reaching ~5–6 m

animal.diet: Almost entirely fish
animal.habitat: Deep, fast-flowing rivers with high sandbanks for basking and nesting
animal.size: Males up to ~5–6 m; females ~3.5–4.5 m
animal.behaviour: Rarely leaves the water except to bask and nest on sandbanks. Hatchlings stay in groups (crèches) guarded by adults, sometimes riding on a large male's back. Its legs are too weak for it to walk upright on land, so it slides on its belly.
fieldMarks: Very long, narrow snout with many interlocking teeth
Bulbous knob (ghara) on the snout tip of adult males
Olive to grey-brown body
Basks on river sandbanks
animal.lookalikes: The mugger crocodile has a broad, heavy snout. The false gharial (Tomistoma schlegelii) of Southeast Asia has a slightly broader snout tapering from the head and lives far away.
animal.whereToSee: National Chambal Sanctuary (Madhya Pradesh–Rajasthan–Uttar Pradesh), Katarniaghat on the Girwa River, Chitwan National Park (Nepal)
animal.season: Resident; best seen basking in winter (Nov–Mar); nesting Mar–Apr; hatching in June

lore: In the 1970s fewer than 200 gharials were left in the wild, and India's Project Crocodile, started in 1975, reared hatchlings from collected eggs for release. In Hindu art, the makara, vehicle of the river goddess Ganga, is often shown with a long snout like a gharial.
funFact: In 2007–08 more than 100 gharials died on the Chambal River from a disease or toxin, which showed how vulnerable a few small populations can be.

summary: A great conservation success: hunted almost to extinction by the mid-20th century, then protected and recovered. It shapes the wetlands of the southeastern US, digging 'gator holes' that hold water and wildlife through the dry season.
nativeRange: Southeastern United States, from North Carolina to Florida and west to Texas, and up the Mississippi valley into Arkansas and Oklahoma
abilities: Digs 'gator holes' that stay wet in the dry season, keeping alive fish, turtles and birds
Survives freezing weather by keeping only its nostrils above ice ('icing')
Males bellow and send infrasound that makes water 'dance' on their backs
Sex of the young is set by nest temperature

animal.diet: Fish, turtles, snakes, birds, mammals; young eat insects and crayfish
animal.habitat: Freshwater marshes, swamps, rivers, lakes, and some brackish water
animal.behaviour: Females build mound nests of rotting vegetation, guard them and carry hatchlings to water in their mouths. Hatchlings call from inside the eggs when ready to hatch.
fieldMarks: Broad, rounded U-shaped snout
Upper jaw covers the lower teeth when the mouth is closed
Dark grey to black; juveniles with yellow bands
Bony plates on the back
animal.lookalikes: The American crocodile (Crocodylus acutus), found only in southern Florida in the US, has a narrow, tapered V-shaped snout, a paler grey-green colour, and a visible fourth lower tooth when its mouth is closed. Caimans (introduced in Florida) are smaller with a bony ridge between the eyes.
animal.whereToSee: Everglades National Park (Anhinga Trail), Okefenokee Swamp, Louisiana's Atchafalaya Basin, Brazos Bend State Park (Texas)
animal.season: Resident; bellowing and courtship April–May; nesting June–July

lore: The name 'alligator' comes from the Spanish el lagarto, 'the lizard'. Listed as endangered in 1967, it was removed from the US endangered list in 1987.
