funFact: The Chinese alligator (Alligator sinensis) is its only living close relative; the two lineages diverged tens of millions of years ago.

summary: Africa's largest predator in fresh water, famous for ambushing wildebeest and zebra at river crossings. It killed and inspired people throughout history and was worshipped in ancient Egypt as the god Sobek.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa, the Nile basin and Madagascar (the West African crocodile, Crocodylus suchus, is now treated as a separate species)
abilities: Ambushes large mammals at the water's edge and drowns them
Can go many months without eating
Females carry hatchlings to the water in their mouths
Groups cooperate to feed on large carcasses, holding and spinning to tear meat

animal.diet: Fish, and mammals up to the size of wildebeest, zebra and buffalo
animal.habitat: Rivers, lakes, swamps and estuaries
animal.size: Males usually 3.5–5 m, exceptionally ~6 m; females smaller
animal.behaviour: Basks with its mouth open to cool down. Females bury eggs in sandbanks and guard them for about three months. It is thought to be responsible for more attacks on people than any other crocodile species.
fieldMarks: Large, olive-bronze crocodile with dark bands on the tail
Broad, V-shaped snout
Fourth lower tooth visible when the mouth is closed
Basks on sandbanks
animal.lookalikes: The West African crocodile (C. suchus) is smaller and found mainly in West and Central Africa. The slender-snouted crocodile (Mecistops) has a long thin snout. Dwarf crocodiles (Osteolaemus) are small and dark.
animal.whereToSee: Mara River crossings (Kenya, Tanzania), Kruger National Park, Lake Chamo (Ethiopia), Okavango Delta, Lake Nasser
animal.season: Resident; wildebeest crossings July–October in the Mara

lore: Ancient Egyptians worshipped the crocodile god Sobek at Kom Ombo and Crocodilopolis (Faiyum), where sacred crocodiles were kept, fed and mummified by the thousands. Herodotus wrote that the plover picked its teeth, a story still repeated today.
funFact: DNA from crocodile mummies from ancient Egypt showed that some were West African crocodiles, perhaps chosen because they are less aggressive and easier to keep in temples.

summary: A broad-snouted crocodile of South Asia's rivers, lakes and reservoirs. It is adaptable and digs burrows to survive drought, and it has been seen balancing sticks on its snout to lure nest-building birds.
nativeRange: India, Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Nepal and southeastern Iran; extinct in Bhutan and probably Myanmar; possibly surviving in Bangladesh
abilities: Digs burrows into riverbanks to escape heat and drought
Has been seen balancing sticks on its snout near egret colonies during the nesting season, possibly to lure birds collecting nest material
Travels overland between water bodies
Lives in reservoirs, irrigation canals and town lakes

animal.diet: Fish, birds, turtles, deer, monkeys and other mammals
animal.habitat: Rivers, lakes, marshes, reservoirs, irrigation canals
animal.size: Males up to ~4–5 m; females ~2.5–3 m
animal.behaviour: Basks for long periods, often with its mouth open. Females dig nests in sandbanks and carry hatchlings to the water.
fieldMarks: Broad, heavy snout, the widest of any living Crocodylus
Grey to olive-brown body; juveniles banded
Fourth lower tooth visible when the mouth is closed
Lacks the pair of bony bumps in front of the eyes seen on saltwater crocodiles
animal.lookalikes: The gharial has a very thin snout. The saltwater crocodile, found in coastal areas such as the Sundarbans, Bhitarkanika and Sri Lankan estuaries, has a longer, narrower snout and bony ridges in front of the eyes.
animal.whereToSee: National Chambal Sanctuary, Ranganathittu Bird Sanctuary (Karnataka), Vishwamitri River (Vadodara), Yala and Wilpattu (Sri Lanka), Bardia (Nepal)
animal.season: Resident; nesting February–April

lore: At the shrine of Pir Mangho in Karachi, muggers have been kept in a pool for centuries and are fed by pilgrims, who consider them the saint's disciples. Rudyard Kipling's 'The Undertakers' (1895) features a mugger of a Ganges village.
funFact: In 2013 Vladimir Dinets reported muggers and American alligators balancing sticks on their snouts near bird colonies, probably the first known tool use by reptiles.

summary: North America's largest true frog, whose deep, booming call carries across summer ponds. It will eat almost anything it can fit in its mouth. Introduced around the world for frog legs, it has become an invasive species that eats native frogs and spreads disease.
nativeRange: Eastern and central North America, from southern Canada to the Gulf of Mexico; introduced in western North America, South America, Europe and East Asia
abilities: Eats insects, crayfish, fish, other frogs, snakes, birds and small mammals
Tadpoles may take one to three years to turn into frogs
Can jump more than ten times its own body length
Can carry chytrid fungus without becoming ill, spreading it to other amphibians

animal.diet: Almost anything it can swallow
animal.habitat: Permanent ponds, lakes and slow rivers with vegetation
animal.size: Body ~9–15 cm; up to ~20 cm and ~0.5 kg
animal.behaviour: Males defend calling territories in summer and wrestle rivals.
fieldMarks: Large green to olive frog, often with darker mottling
Large round eardrum (tympanum), bigger than the eye in males
A ridge curving around the eardrum but no ridges down the back
Males have a yellow throat
animal.voice: A deep, resonant 'jug-o-rum' or bellowing 'rumm', like a foghorn or bull; heard on summer nights
animal.lookalikes: The green frog (L. clamitans) has a pair of ridges (dorsolateral folds) running down its back and calls a twangy 'gunk', like a loose banjo string. The pig frog (L. grylio) of the Southeast has a grunting call and a more pointed snout.
animal.whereToSee: Ponds, lakes and marshes across the eastern US and southern Canada
animal.season: Calls May–August; hibernates underwater in winter

edibilityNote: Hind legs are eaten and the species is farmed for meat. Cook thoroughly. Wild frogs from polluted water may carry contaminants.
lore: Mark Twain's 1865 story 'The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County' inspired the jumping frog contest held at the Calaveras County Fair since 1928, where bullfrogs are the usual competitors.
funFact: Bullfrogs released in Japan in 1918 for food spread across the islands, and they are now listed in Japan as an invasive alien species.

summary: A heavy, warty toad of tropical America that was released in Australia, the Caribbean and the Pacific to control cane beetles. It failed at that and instead spread its poison through native wildlife. Its skin glands produce bufotoxins that can kill dogs, quolls, goannas and snakes that bite it.
nativeRange: Southern Texas and Mexico through Central America to the central Amazon; introduced in Australia, the Caribbean, Hawaii, Florida, the Philippines, Papua New Guinea and many islands
abilities: Large glands behind the eyes (parotoids) produce bufadienolide toxins that can stop the heart of predators
Eggs and tadpoles are toxic too
Has spread across northern Australia at up to ~50 km per year
Breeds in almost any still water, laying up to 30,000 eggs at a time

animal.diet: Insects, snails, small vertebrates, pet food and garbage
animal.habitat: Open habitats near water, farmland, gardens and towns
animal.behaviour: When threatened it puffs up and tilts its glands toward the attacker. Pets that mouth a toad may drool, collapse and die: wipe the gums with a damp cloth (do not hose into the throat) and get to a vet at once. People who handle toads should wash their hands. Never lick or eat toads or eggs; people have died from eating them.
fieldMarks: Large, warty, brown toad with dry skin
Huge triangular parotoid glands behind the eyes
Bony ridges above the eyes meeting at the snout
Unwebbed fingers, webbed toes
animal.voice: A long, low trill like a dial tone or a distant idling motor, lasting several seconds
animal.lookalikes: In Australia, native frogs such as giant banjo frogs (Limnodynastes) and burrowing frogs have no large parotoid glands or bony head ridges. In the US the Gulf Coast toad (Incilius nebulifer) is smaller with a light stripe down the back.
animal.whereToSee: Introduced: Queensland and the Northern Territory (Australia), Florida, Hawaii; native: Central and South American lowlands
animal.season: Active year-round in the tropics; breeds mostly in the wet season

edibilityNote: Skin, glands and eggs are deadly poisonous; people have died after eating toads or toad eggs.
lore: In 1935, 102 cane toads were brought from Hawaii to Gordonvale, Queensland, to control cane beetles. Their descendants have spread across more than 1.2 million square kilometres of Australia.
funFact: In parts of Australia, crows and native water rats (rakali) have learned to flip cane toads over and eat them from the belly side, avoiding the poison glands.

summary: Northern Europe's familiar brown frog, found from Mediterranean mountains to beyond the Arctic Circle. Each spring it is one of the first amphibians to breed, filling ponds with clumps of spawn.
nativeRange: Most of Europe from northern Spain and Britain to the Urals and western Siberia, north beyond the Arctic Circle; absent from much of the Mediterranean lowland
abilities: Breeds in water as cold as just above freezing
Lives at altitudes up to ~2,500 m in the Alps
Can change skin tone to match its surroundings over hours or days

animal.diet: Insects, slugs, snails, worms, spiders; tadpoles graze algae
animal.habitat: Ponds, ditches, marshes, damp grassland, woodland and gardens
animal.behaviour: Large numbers gather in ponds in early spring for a few days of 'explosive' breeding, often in the same pond each year.
fieldMarks: Brown, olive or yellow-brown with variable dark spots
Dark 'mask' patch behind the eye over the eardrum
Dark bars on the hind legs
Smooth, moist skin; hops rather than crawls
animal.voice: A low, soft, purring croak, like a distant motorbike, often from many frogs together
animal.lookalikes: The common toad (Bufo bufo) has warty skin, crawls and lays spawn in strings, not clumps. The moor frog (R. arvalis) has a more pointed snout and males can turn blue when breeding. The agile frog (R. dalmatina) has very long hind legs and a paler body.
animal.whereToSee: Garden ponds and wetlands across Britain, Ireland, Scandinavia and the Alps
animal.season: Spawns February–April (later in the north and mountains); hibernates in winter, males often in pond mud

funFact: In Ireland it is the only native frog; whether it arrived naturally or with medieval monks has long been debated.

summary: A leaf-green tree frog of Central American rainforests with scarlet eyes, blue-and-yellow flanks and orange feet. Its unborn tadpoles can hatch early when they sense the vibrations of a snake attacking their eggs.
nativeRange: Lowland rainforests from southern Mexico through Central America to northwestern Colombia
abilities: Embryos hatch up to several days early to escape snakes or wasps, telling attack vibrations from rain
Startles predators by suddenly opening its bright red eyes and flashing its coloured flanks
Lays eggs on leaves over water, so hatching tadpoles drop straight in

animal.diet: Crickets, moths, flies and other insects
animal.habitat: Rainforest trees near ponds and swamps
animal.behaviour: By day it sleeps on the underside of a leaf with eyes closed and bright colours tucked away, appearing all green. Males call from branches over ponds on rainy nights.
fieldMarks: Bright green with large red eyes and vertical pupils
Blue to purple flanks with pale vertical bars
Orange or red toes with suction-cup pads
Slender body and long limbs
animal.voice: A short 'chack' or 'chack-chack', repeated at intervals from vegetation above water
animal.lookalikes: Morelet's tree frog (A. moreletii) has dark red eyes and no bars on its flanks. The gliding leaf frog (A. spurrelli) has large webbed hands and spots on the back.
animal.whereToSee: La Selva, Tortuguero and Sarapiquí (Costa Rica), Panama's Soberanía National Park, Belize; ponds on rainy-season nights
animal.season: Breeds in the rainy season (May–November)

lore: Its picture has become a symbol of rainforest conservation, appearing on countless posters and stamps since the 1980s.
funFact: Karen Warkentin's research showed that red-eyed tree frog embryos can tell the vibration pattern of a snake attack from rain and hatch in seconds.

summary: Probably the most poisonous animal on Earth for its size. This thumb-sized yellow, orange or mint-green frog lives in a few rainforest valleys of Colombia's Pacific coast. Its skin holds batrachotoxin, which Emberá hunters used to poison blowgun darts.
nativeRange: Pacific lowland rainforest of Cauca department, Colombia
abilities: Its skin contains batrachotoxin, which keeps sodium channels in nerves and muscle open and can cause fatal heart failure
A single wild frog is estimated to carry enough toxin to kill about ten people
Has resistant sodium channels so it is not harmed by its own poison
Gets its toxin from its wild diet; captive-bred frogs are harmless

animal.diet: Ants, beetles and other small invertebrates
animal.habitat: Leaf litter of humid lowland rainforest near streams
animal.behaviour: Active by day and bold because of its toxin. Males carry tadpoles on their backs to water. Wild frogs must never be touched: toxin on the skin can enter through cuts.
fieldMarks: Uniform bright yellow, orange or pale metallic green
Black eyes; often black spots on the toe tips
Larger than most poison frogs
Active in daylight on the forest floor
animal.voice: A long series of rapid trills given by males
animal.lookalikes: The Kokoe poison frog (P. aurotaenia) is black with orange or green stripes. The black-legged poison frog (P. bicolor) is yellow-orange with dark legs and is smaller.
animal.whereToSee: Only in a few areas in Cauca, Colombia (Rio Saija drainage); best seen in zoos
animal.season: Resident

lore: The Emberá people of Colombia rub blowgun darts on the backs of living frogs to poison them, without killing the frogs. Scientists Charles Myers, John Daly and Borys Malkin described the species in 1978.
funFact: Batrachotoxin is also found in the feathers of some New Guinea birds, the pitohuis and blue-capped ifrit, which probably get it from beetles.

summary: A small, lime-green frog of Central and South American streamsides whose belly is so transparent that its beating heart can be seen. Males guard egg clutches on the undersides of leaves hanging over the water.
nativeRange: Southern Mexico through Central America to Colombia, Ecuador and Venezuela (some northern South American populations have been split as separate species)
abilities: When sleeping it hides almost 90% of its red blood cells in its liver, becoming two to three times more transparent
Its translucent body helps it blend into leaves by softening its outline
Males guard eggs for weeks, protecting them from wasps and fungus

animal.diet: Small insects and spiders
animal.habitat: Vegetation along streams in lowland and montane rainforest
animal.behaviour: Males call from the underside of leaves over streams on rainy nights and guard the eggs. Hatching tadpoles drop into the stream below.
fieldMarks: Small, flat frog, lime-green with tiny yellow spots
Translucent belly through which the heart and organs can be seen
Large eyes facing forward, with gold irises
Often found on the undersides of leaves over streams
animal.voice: A high-pitched, rising 'peep' or 'wheet', repeated at intervals
animal.lookalikes: Many glass frogs look alike. The reticulated glass frog (H. valerioi) has a net of yellow lines on its back. Emerald glass frogs (Espadarana prosoblepon) have green bones and a white spine on the arm of males. A close view of the underside and the call help with identification.
animal.whereToSee: Streams at La Selva, Monteverde and Arenal (Costa Rica), Panama's Chiriquí highlands; night walks in the rainy season
animal.season: Breeds in the rainy season

lore: Oskar Boettger described it in 1893 from Costa Rican specimens and named it after Carl Fleischmann, who collected them.
funFact: A 2022 study in Science showed that sleeping frogs of this species pack red blood cells into their liver without blood clots forming, which interests researchers studying clotting disorders.

summary: A brown, masked frog of northern forests that freezes solid in winter. Its heart stops and much of its body water turns to ice, and it thaws back to life in spring. It ranges farther north than any other North American amphibian, beyond the Arctic Circle.
nativeRange: Alaska and Canada to the Arctic treeline, south to the Appalachians and northeastern US
abilities: Survives being frozen, with up to about two-thirds of its body water turned to ice
Floods its cells with glucose and urea, which act as antifreeze
Alaskan wood frogs survive temperatures as low as −16 °C
Breeds in temporary pools free of fish

animal.diet: Insects, spiders, slugs, snails and worms
animal.habitat: Moist woodland, breeding in vernal pools and ponds
animal.behaviour: In early spring, sometimes while ice still covers part of the pond, wood frogs gather for a breeding frenzy that lasts only a few days, laying large egg masses together.
fieldMarks: Brown, tan or rust frog with a dark mask through the eye
White line along the upper lip
Ridges (dorsolateral folds) running down the back
Often a pale stripe down the middle of the back
animal.voice: A chorus of short, rasping clucks, like quacking ducks
animal.lookalikes: Leopard frogs (L. pipiens) are green or brown with large dark spots. Pickerel frogs have squarish spots. The spring peeper is tiny with an X on its back. The wood frog's dark mask is distinctive.
animal.whereToSee: Vernal pools in New England, the Great Lakes region, Ontario, Quebec, Alaska; listen in early spring
animal.season: Breeds March–May (as soon as ice melts); hibernates frozen in leaf litter in winter

funFact: A frozen wood frog shows no heartbeat or breathing. Within hours of thawing its heart starts again.

summary: A bloated, purple-grey frog with a pointed pig-like snout that spends most of its life underground in India's Western Ghats, surfacing only for a few days in the monsoon to breed. Its closest relatives live in the Seychelles, a link to the breakup of Gondwana.
nativeRange: Western Ghats of India (Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka)
abilities: Lives buried up to several metres underground for most of the year
Feeds on termites and ants in their underground tunnels, probing with its pointed snout
Tadpoles cling to rocks in fast monsoon streams with sucker-like mouths
Its lineage split from its Seychelles relatives tens of millions of years ago

animal.diet: Termites, also ants
animal.habitat: Moist forest and plantations near seasonal streams
animal.behaviour: Emerges for a few days in the pre-monsoon or early monsoon to breed in fast-flowing streams. The small male clings to the larger female's back.
fieldMarks: Bloated, purplish-grey body
Small head with a pointed pig-like snout
Short limbs adapted for digging
Small eyes
animal.voice: A soft, chicken-like 'cluck', given from underground or at stream edges in the early monsoon
animal.lookalikes: No other Indian frog looks like it. The Bhupathy's purple frog (N. bhupathi), described in 2017, is similar and lives in the eastern slopes of the southern Western Ghats; it breeds later, during the northeast monsoon.
animal.whereToSee: Monsoon streams in Kerala's Idukki district and the Western Ghats; rarely seen
animal.season: Emerges for a few days in May–June to breed

lore: S. D. Biju and Franky Bossuyt described the purple frog in Nature in 2003, revealing a new family of frogs. In Kerala it has been proposed as the state frog, and local people call it 'Mahabali' after the legendary king who returns from the underworld once a year.
funFact: Local people knew the purple frog long before scientists; its tadpoles are collected and eaten in parts of Kerala.

summary: A glossy black-and-yellow salamander of European forests, out mainly on rainy nights. Its skin secretes toxic alkaloids, and its colours warn predators. It is now threatened by a fungus, Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans, which has wiped out populations in the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany.
nativeRange: Central and southern Europe, from Iberia to the Balkans and the Carpathians
abilities: Secretes samandarin, a neurotoxic alkaloid, from glands in its skin
Can squirt toxic secretions from glands along its spine
Females give birth to live larvae in cool streams; some populations give birth to fully formed young
Can live for decades

animal.diet: Worms, slugs, insects, spiders
animal.habitat: Damp deciduous forests near clean streams, in hilly or mountain country
animal.lifespan: ~20 years in the wild; 50+ in captivity
animal.behaviour: Active at night, especially after rain. Its toxin is harmful if swallowed and stings eyes and mouth, so wash your hands after touching one.
fieldMarks: Glossy black with bold yellow (or orange or red) spots or stripes
Large parotoid glands behind the eyes
Rows of glands along the back
Stocky body, short tail
animal.lookalikes: The Alpine salamander (S. atra) is all black and lives high in the Alps. The Corsican and Near Eastern fire salamanders are separate species with their own ranges. North American spotted salamanders (Ambystoma maculatum) are dark with yellow spots but live on another continent.
animal.whereToSee: Beech forests of Germany, Switzerland, France, northern Spain and the Balkans; wet nights in spring and autumn
animal.season: Active spring to autumn on rainy nights; larvae born in spring

lore: Pliny the Elder wrote that the salamander was so cold that it could put out fires, and medieval bestiaries and Paracelsus made it the elemental spirit of fire. The belief probably arose from salamanders crawling out of logs thrown on the fire.
funFact: François I of France chose a salamander in flames as his emblem, with the motto 'Nutrisco et extinguo' ('I nourish and extinguish'); it is carved all over the Château de Chambord.

summary: Among the largest amphibians alive, recorded at up to 1.8 m. This brown, wrinkled salamander lives in cold mountain streams of China. It is Critically Endangered, mainly because of hunting and farming for meat, and farm-bred animals of mixed origin have been released into wild rivers.
nativeRange: Mountain streams of central and southern China; genetic studies suggest the old 'davidianus' is several species (A. sligoi, A. jiangxiensis and others), with A. davidianus in the narrow sense restricted to part of this range
abilities: Breathes mainly through its wrinkled skin
Detects prey with sensory nodes along its head and body, sensing water movement
Can live for decades; over 50 years in captivity
Males guard eggs in underwater dens

animal.diet: Fish, frogs, crabs, shrimp, worms, insects
animal.habitat: Clear, cold, rocky mountain streams and rivers
animal.size: Usually ~1 m; historically up to ~1.8 m
animal.behaviour: Hides by day in crevices and dens and ambushes prey at night with a fast suction gulp.
fieldMarks: Huge, flattened, brown salamander with wrinkled skin
Broad, flat head with tiny eyes
Fold of skin along the sides of the body
Short limbs
animal.lookalikes: The Japanese giant salamander (A. japonicus) is very similar and lives only in Japan; the two are best told apart by where they are found. The North American hellbender (Cryptobranchus) is much smaller.
animal.whereToSee: Rarely seen in the wild; nature reserves in Zhangjiajie (Hunan), Shaanxi's Qinling Mountains; also in zoos
animal.season: Resident; breeds in late summer

lore: Its Chinese name 'baby fish' refers to its cry, said to sound like a human baby. It was described in 1871 from specimens sent by the French missionary-naturalist Armand David.
funFact: Millions are raised on farms in China for meat, but surveys across its range found few wild animals left.

summary: A blind, pale-pink salamander that spends its whole life in the dark underground waters of the Dinaric Karst. It keeps its feathery larval gills for life, can live for more than a century and may go years without eating. A 2026 study split the olm into nine species, and iNaturalist now restricts Proteus anguinus to one of these lineages; the account here covers the olm group as a whole.
nativeRange: Underground waters of the Dinaric Karst from northeastern Italy and Slovenia through Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina (the olm group as a whole)
abilities: Can live for 100 years or more
Survives years without food
Senses light through its skin and detects electric and magnetic fields
Keeps external gills as an adult (neoteny)

animal.diet: Small crustaceans, snails and insect larvae
animal.habitat: Cold, clean underground streams and lakes in limestone caves
animal.behaviour: Extremely inactive: one olm in a Bosnian cave was recorded in the same spot for more than seven years.
fieldMarks: Long, eel-like, pale pink-white body
Bright red feathery external gills
Tiny skin-covered eyes
Three toes on the front feet and two on the back
animal.lookalikes: The black olm (P. parkelj) of Bela Krajina in Slovenia is dark-skinned, with eyes. No other European amphibian lives permanently in caves.
animal.whereToSee: Postojna Cave (Slovenia), which has a viewing aquarium; Tular Cave Laboratory in Kranj
animal.season: Resident

lore: In 1689 Johann Weikhard von Valvasor wrote in 'The Glory of the Duchy of Carniola' that locals believed olms washed out of caves after floods were the young of dragons living underground.
funFact: In 2016 a female olm in Postojna Cave laid eggs that hatched under the care of the cave's biologists, a very rare breeding record for the species.

summary: A tiny frog whose two-note 'ko-KEE' call fills Puerto Rico's nights and has become a national symbol. Its eggs hatch directly into froglets with no tadpole stage. In Hawaii, where it was introduced, it is an invasive pest whose loud choruses cause complaints.
nativeRange: Puerto Rico; introduced to Hawaii, the US Virgin Islands, Florida and elsewhere
abilities: Eggs hatch directly into tiny froglets, with no tadpole or need for standing water
Males guard eggs and keep them moist
Its call can reach about 90 decibels at half a metre
Climbs using toe pads, with no webbing between its toes

animal.diet: Insects, spiders, snails
animal.habitat: Forest, gardens and towns, from sea level to mountains
animal.behaviour: Males call from leaves and tree trunks at dusk to attract females and defend their territory.
fieldMarks: Small brown or grey frog, often with a pale stripe or W-shaped mark
Large toe pads, no webbing
Large eyes
Loud two-note call
animal.voice: A loud, two-note 'ko-KEE', the first note lower, repeated through the night
animal.lookalikes: Puerto Rico has around 16 other Eleutherodactylus species, many of them small and brown, so the common coquí's two-note call is the best way to identify it.
animal.whereToSee: El Yunque National Forest and almost anywhere in Puerto Rico at night; Hawaii's Big Island
animal.season: Calls year-round, loudest in the wet season

lore: In Puerto Rico people say 'Soy de aquí como el coquí' ('I'm from here, like the coquí'), and the frog appears in Taíno petroglyphs.
funFact: Coquís at higher altitudes in Puerto Rico are larger and have deeper calls than those in the lowlands.

summary: South Asia's largest frog. During the first monsoon rains the males turn bright yellow and puff out blue vocal sacs, calling in loud choruses. It was exported in huge numbers for frog legs until India banned the trade in 1987.
nativeRange: Afghanistan and Pakistan through India, Nepal and Bangladesh to Myanmar; introduced to the Andaman Islands and Madagascar
abilities: Males turn bright yellow and show blue vocal sacs in the breeding season
Can leap long distances and skitter across water
Eats almost anything it can fit into its mouth, including other frogs, snakes and small birds

animal.diet: Insects, crabs, fish, frogs, snakes, small birds and rodents
animal.habitat: Ponds, marshes, rice paddies and ditches
animal.behaviour: Comes out in large numbers to breed after the first monsoon rains; males call from shallow water.
fieldMarks: Large olive-green to brown frog with dark spots
Thin yellow line down the middle of the back
Breeding males bright yellow with blue vocal sacs
Pointed snout and strongly webbed toes
animal.voice: A loud, hoarse croak, given in deafening choruses after the monsoon rains
animal.lookalikes: Jerdon's bullfrog (H. crassus) has shorter hind limbs and a shorter snout. Skittering frogs (Euphlyctis) are smaller and more aquatic.
animal.whereToSee: Rice paddies and ponds across the Indian plains; Keoladeo (Bharatpur) and Sundarbans; best seen at the onset of the monsoon
animal.season: Breeding with the first monsoon rains (June–July)

edibilityNote: Eaten locally; commercial frog-leg export is banned in India, and catching wild frogs is illegal there. Cook thoroughly.
lore: The Rigveda's frog hymn (Maṇḍūka Sūkta, 7.103) compares frogs croaking at the start of the monsoon to priests chanting; South Asia's monsoon chorus of bullfrogs is the sound it describes.
funFact: Before India banned exports in 1987, tens of millions of frogs were exported every year, and some studies linked the loss of frogs to increases in crop pests and mosquitoes.
